summaries.example: Imagine someone is connected to another sick person’s body so the sick person can stay alive. Even if the sick person has a right to live, philosophers may ask whether the first person must keep providing bodily help. This thought experiment is used to think about abortion.
summaries.summary: The ethics of abortion asks whether ending a pregnancy is morally wrong. Philosophers examine several arguments. One says a fetus has a right to life. Another says abortion takes away a valuable future. Other arguments use the Golden Rule, the value of human life, the chance of making a serious moral mistake, or concerns about discrimination against disabled people. The entry also presents replies to these arguments. It explains that even if abortion is morally wrong, a separate question remains: should it be illegal? The discussion matters because pregnancy and parenthood affect a person’s body, choices, health, and future.
key_ideas: The entry asks whether abortion is morally wrong, while separating that question from whether governments should make abortion illegal.
One argument says abortion is wrong because a fetus may be a person with a right to life. Critics question what “person” means and what a right to life requires.
Another argument says abortion takes away a valuable possible future. Critics ask whether an early fetus has that future in the same way an older person does.

The violinist thought experiment asks whether someone must use their body to keep another person alive. It is meant to show that a right to life may not always include a right to use another person’s body.
Other arguments discuss the Golden Rule, the value of human life, the risk of making a serious moral mistake, and whether some abortions express unfair ideas about disability.
The entry says abortion matters because pregnancy, parenthood, and control over one’s life can be very important.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because people disagree about a serious decision that can affect bodies, families, health, and life plans. Studying the arguments helps us notice hidden assumptions, listen carefully to opposing views, and distinguish a moral question from a legal one. The entry does not treat the disagreement as simple or settled.

important_terms.definition: A moral question asks what is right or wrong, fair or unfair, or good or bad to do.
Moral status means being someone or something whose interests should count in our decisions.
A right to life is a claim that someone should not be killed unjustly.
A valuable future is a future containing things that may be good for someone, such as experiences, relationships, and activities.
Autonomy means having an important say over your own body and major life choices.

questions_to_think_about: Does having a right to live always mean having a right to use someone else’s body?
Is being able to become a person enough to have the same moral status as a person now?
Can two people agree that human life is valuable but disagree about what should happen in difficult cases?
Why might a reason for an abortion matter morally, even if someone thinks abortion is sometimes allowed?

summaries.example: Consider a person unexpectedly attached to a violinist whose life depends on using that person’s kidneys for nine months. The person was connected without permission and may detach, even though detaching causes the violinist’s death. The case challenges the inference that a right to life automatically creates a right to another person’s bodily support. Critics ask whether pregnancy differs when sex was consensual or when the pregnant person is responsible for the dependence.
summaries.summary: The entry surveys competing arguments about the moral status of abortion rather than presenting a single settled answer. The right-to-life argument claims that a fetus is a person, persons have a right to life, and abortion is wrong because it kills the fetus. Objections challenge the meaning of “person,” the duties generated by a right to life, the relevance of potentiality, the role of consciousness, and an argument based on miscarriage. The violinist case argues that even a being with a right to life may lack a right to another person’s bodily support. The argument from loss instead focuses on deprivation of a valuable future, while its critics dispute whether an early fetus presently possesses such a future or has the moral status required for the loss to make killing wrong. Further arguments appeal to the Golden Rule, intrinsic value, moral uncertainty, and possible discrimination in selective abortion. Finally, the entry emphasizes that the moral issue is distinct from the legal question of restriction and connects abortion to bodily autonomy and control over parenthood.
key_ideas: The right-to-life argument depends on controversial premises: that the fetus is a person in the relevant sense, that persons have a right to life, and that abortion is an unjust killing.
The equivocation objection distinguishes “human being” from “moral person.” The argument is persuasive only by treating “person” as if it had the same meaning in every premise.

The violinist case grants, for purposes of argument, that the fetus has a right to life. It argues that this right may not include a right to another person’s bodily aid, so abortion might still be permissible.
Arguments from potentiality, self-consciousness, consciousness, and miscarriage challenge the claim that an early fetus already has full moral status.

The argument from loss avoids directly claiming that a fetus is a person: abortion is said to be wrong because it removes a valuable future. Objections say that a valuable future matters morally only together with moral status, or that early fetuses lack the psychological connections needed to possess such a future now.

The entry also examines arguments from the Golden Rule, intrinsic value, and moral risk, plus an expressive argument that some selective abortions may communicate discriminatory attitudes toward disability. Each receives objections.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters because philosophical conclusions can affect how people understand bodily rights, parenthood, disability, responsibility, and public policy. The entry stresses that legal conclusions do not follow automatically from a moral argument. It also argues that the significance of abortion cannot be reduced to the physical burdens of pregnancy: access can affect whether and when people become parents and how they direct their lives.

important_terms.definition: A person, in one use, is a human being; in another, a being with full moral status. Switching between these meanings can create an equivocation.
Moral status is the degree to which a being’s interests count directly in moral reasoning; full moral status is the status ordinarily assigned to adult humans.
A right to life is not necessarily a right to every resource needed for survival; the entry considers it more plausibly a right not to be killed unjustly.
Potentiality is the capacity to become a being with some feature later. The entry examines whether potential full moral status gives that status now.
The future-like-ours view holds that killing is wrong partly because it deprives someone of a valuable future connected to that person through psychological continuity.
Pro tanto wrong means wrong unless there is a sufficient justification; an argument can identify a serious reason against an act without deciding the final all-things-considered judgment.
Moral risk is the risk of doing something seriously wrong because one may be mistaken in one’s moral reasoning.
Autonomy is a person’s authority to make important decisions about their own body and whether, and when, to become a parent.

questions_to_think_about: If a fetus has a right to life, what kind of duty does that create for the pregnant person: a duty not to kill, a duty to provide aid, or something else?
Does moral status depend on current abilities, future development, consciousness, psychological continuity, or another feature?
Is losing a valuable future morally significant even when the being who loses it has little or no psychological connection to that future?
Can an abortion be morally permissible in general but objectionable when chosen for a particular reason?
How should moral reasoning handle uncertainty when the burdens of continuing a pregnancy are substantial?

summaries.example: Suppose you agree to help a sick musician, but before the help begins you discover that the musician will need your body for nine months. You may decide that the sacrifice is too great. Now imagine that someone secretly connects you to the musician anyway. A philosopher uses this case to ask whether saving a life always gives someone permission to use another person’s body. People may then debate whether the case is similar to pregnancy, especially when sex was consensual.
summaries.summary: The entry presents a range of philosophical arguments about whether abortion is morally wrong and the replies those arguments receive. The central right-to-life argument depends on claims about personhood, moral status, and unjust killing. Its critics question whether “person” has been used consistently, whether a right to life includes a right to another person’s bodily support, and whether potential, consciousness, or self-awareness are enough for full moral status. The violinist thought experiment supports a bodily-autonomy response, although responsibility for consensual sex is raised as a challenge. A different argument says abortion is wrong because it deprives a fetus of a valuable future; objections focus on moral status and the weak psychological connection of an early fetus to its future. Other arguments use the Golden Rule, intrinsic value, moral risk, and concerns about disability-related discrimination. The entry ends by explaining why abortion affects autonomy and the timing of parenthood, while noting that moral and legal questions are not identical.
key_ideas: The source focuses on the moral question of abortion. It says the separate legal and political question—whether abortion should be restricted—is important but not its main topic.
The right-to-life argument says that if the fetus is a person and all persons have a right to life, abortion is wrong. Critics say the argument may use two meanings of “person.”
The violinist case suggests that having a right to life does not automatically mean having a right to someone else’s body. A response asks whether responsibility for pregnancy changes the situation.
Some philosophers argue that potential personhood is not the same as present full moral status. Others focus on consciousness, self-awareness, or what happens in cases of miscarriage.

The loss argument says abortion prevents a valuable future. Critics reply that this may secretly depend on giving the fetus moral status, or that an early fetus is not psychologically connected to its future like an existing person is.

The entry considers additional arguments about treating others as we wish to be treated, the value of human life, moral uncertainty, and whether abortions based on disability can express unfair judgments. It also explains replies to each.
summaries.why_it_matters: Abortion is a sensitive issue involving competing claims about life, bodily control, responsibility, family, and fairness. Learning the arguments can show why reasonable people may disagree and how a conclusion can depend on a particular definition or hidden premise. It also encourages careful discussion without assuming that a moral judgment automatically settles what laws should say.

important_terms.definition: A moral argument is a set of reasons meant to support a judgment about what someone ought or ought not do.
A person can mean a human being, or it can mean a being with full moral standing. An argument may go wrong if it quietly changes between these meanings.
Moral status describes how much a being’s interests count when we decide what is right to do.
Potentiality is having the possibility of becoming something later; philosophers debate whether that is enough to have its moral status now.
Bodily autonomy is a person’s authority to make decisions about their own body, including whether to provide bodily support.
A valuable future is a future containing worthwhile experiences and activities that someone may otherwise get to have.
Moral risk is the possibility that an action is seriously wrong even after someone has tried to reason carefully about it.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between being biologically human and having full moral status?
Does being responsible for a situation always mean someone must continue providing bodily help?
Why might an argument about abortion be strong against abortion but not prove that abortion is wrong in every case?
Can an action be wrong because of what it expresses, even if the action does not directly harm another person?
Why should people separate a question about what is morally right from a question about what the law should allow?
